title: Wisdom for every day (Proverbs 9:10; Sirach 6:14)
hook: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; a faithful friend is a strong defense

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ecclesiastes' fourteen pairs: a time to weep and a time to laugh. Your line was a time for every purpose. Which season did you name? Day four hundred thirty-four, the end of the week.

Proverbs chapter nine sets up two dinner invitations. The first comes from Wisdom, pictured as a woman. In the Douay-Rheims: "Wisdom hath built herself a house, she hath hewn her out seven pillars." She's slaughtered the meat, mixed the wine, set the table, and sent her servants up to the high places of the town to call out: whoever is simple, come in here. Across town, another woman, called Folly, sits at her own door and calls out to the same people walking by, almost word for word. Same street. Same passersby. Two open doors.
screen: `TWO DINNER INVITATIONS.` → `A HOUSE OF SEVEN PILLARS.` → `FOLLY CALLS THE SAME PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Between the two invitations is the line the whole book of Proverbs leans on: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Fear here isn't terror. It's closer to awe, the reverence that knows God is God and I'm not. Catholics count fear of the Lord among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, from the Isaiah passage we read a couple of weeks ago. Wisdom starts there, and then it gets very practical. Which brings us to a second wisdom book, one that's in Catholic Bibles: Sirach, also called Ecclesiasticus. It was written in Hebrew by a teacher in Jerusalem, Jesus son of Sirach, around two centuries before Christ, and his grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt. The Latin name Ecclesiasticus is usually explained as the church book, because the early Church used it to teach. In chapter six he talks about friends with real street sense. Some friends are friends for their own convenience, he says, and won't stay in the day of your trouble. Some sit at your table and vanish when things go bad. Test a friend before you trust him. And then: "A faithful friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found him, hath found a treasure." Nothing can be weighed against a faithful friend, he adds; such a friend is medicine for life. For centuries the Hebrew of Sirach was lost, until in the 1890s pages of it turned up in a storeroom of old manuscripts in a Cairo synagogue. Look back at this week: Micah's careful walk, Jonah running and sulking, Job's friends sitting silent, the whirlwind, the seasons, and now wisdom in a friend. A week of learning how to live with God and with each other.
screen: `FEAR OF THE LORD: AWE, NOT TERROR.` · `SIRACH, THE CHURCH BOOK.` · `FRIENDS WHO VANISH IN TROUBLE.` · `LOST HEBREW, FOUND IN CAIRO.` · then, large: `HE HATH FOUND A TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a faithful friend. Settle, and breathe. Think of the friend who stayed in the day of your trouble. Not the one who was fun at the table, though you might love them too; the one who was there when it went bad. Picture their face. Remember one specific thing they did: a phone call, a ride, a long silence beside you, a hard truth told kindly. Let gratitude come. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. Then decide how you'll tell them today, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Wisdom for every day. Proverbs' beginning, the fear of the Lord, and Sirach's practical wisdom: a faithful friend is a strong defense and a treasure. Today's word.
Your line: a friend is treasure. Today, send that faithful friend a message that says thank you, and name the thing they did. Day four hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Proverbs and Sirach in the Mass readings, especially on weekdays, and the Church counts fear of the Lord among the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit received in confirmation.

myth: Ecclesiasticus and Ecclesiastes are the same book
Ecclesiastes is Qoheleth; Ecclesiasticus is Sirach, written by Jesus son of Sirach.
the fear of the Lord in Proverbs means being terrified of God
it's closer to awe and reverence, and Catholics count it among the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
Hebrew pages of Sirach were found in a Cairo synagogue's storeroom in the 1890s
for centuries the book was known mainly in Greek and Latin.

fork.setup: you're walking through town. Wisdom calls from her house of seven pillars: come in. a few doors down, Folly calls you with almost the same words. what do you do?
options: go wherever the louder voice is.
fork.reveal: both invitations sound alike; Proverbs says the difference begins with the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

original.note: Hebrew: fear, awe, reverence, as in the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom.

trapdoor: what you thought: proverbs are fortune-cookie sayings.
what it means: wisdom starts in awe of God and turns very practical, down to which friends will stay when things go bad.
what a scholar hears: Sirach, by Jesus ben Sira around 180 BC, translated by his grandson; much of its Hebrew resurfaced in the Cairo Genizah from 1896, and more at Masada.
